newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Food guru urges heavy fertilizer use in Africa.
newsitem.headline: Food guru urges heavy fertilizer use in Africa.

text.p: Nobel peace laureate Norman Borlaug, main architect of the "green revolution", called on Friday for a dramatic increase in fertilizer use as the key to meeting Africa's famine problems.

"Given present scientific know-how, the use of chemical fertilizers must be quadrupled in sub-Saharan Africa over the next 20 years," Borlaug said in an address to the Fertilizer Society of South Africa.

"Raising the average use of plant nutrients in sub-Saharan Africa from around 10 kg per hectare to something like 40 kg per hectare cannot be an environmental problem, only central to the environmental solution," he said.

Borlaug, 82, won the Nobel peace prize in 1970 for his role in developing high-yield cereal varieties. The work of the U.S. scientist was central to the "green revolution" of the 1960s and 70s that led to India becoming self-sufficient in food.

The dependence of the new crop varieties on heavy doses of fertilizer has been criticised by some development workers who fear the contamination of ground water and who say fertilizer imports are too expensive for poor nations.

Borlaug dismissed these critics as "the anti-technology crowd... noisy, extremist environmentalists" and said the organic cropping methods they advocated would never meet the food needs of the world's expanding population.
"The most severe food-deficit region is sub-Saharan Africa where I doubt I will live to see a green revolution even though the ingredients are already available," he said.

Borlaug, citing research that the region could have 53 million malnourished children by the year 2020, said Africa should not try to grow more food by ploughing virgin bush but should increase the productivity of land already under cultivation.
"Chemical fertilizers should be at the core of soil fertility restoration strategies," he said.

He said Ethiopia, struck by widespread famine in the 1980s, had taken the fertilizer route and had increased cereal and pulse production by 50 percent between 1994 and 1996. Fertilizer imports to Ethiopia had risen from 72,000 tonnes in 1993 to 193,000 in 1996.

"Policy planners have failed to fully understand the impact that the introduction of high-yielding food crop technologies can have on poverty reduction and on making agriculture the engine for economic development," Borlaug said.
